content: This is an updated version of the original Cochrane Review published in 2014. Epilepsy is a prevalent neurological disorder characterized by recurrent seizures. Pharmacological treatment remains the primary approach for managing epilepsy. Sulthiame (STM) is a widely used antiepileptic drug in Europe and Israel. This review summarizes the evidence regarding the use of STM as monotherapy for epilepsy. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and side effect profile of STM as monotherapy in comparison to placebo or other antiepileptic drugs in individuals with epilepsy. The search for relevant studies was conducted on April 13, 2020, using multiple databases, including the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS Web), MEDLINE, PubMed, Embase, ClinicalTrials.gov, the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL). No language restrictions were applied. Additionally, the manufacturers of STM and researchers in the field were contacted to inquire about ongoing or unpublished studies. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials of STM monotherapy in individuals of any age with epilepsy of any cause. Standard Cochrane methodology was followed for data collection and analysis. Two independent reviewers selected the trials and extracted relevant data. The outcomes assessed included treatment withdrawal, seizure freedom at six months, adverse effects, and quality of life. Primary analyses were conducted on an intention-to-treat basis, and a narrative analysis of the data was presented. Four studies involving a total of 355 participants were included in the review. Three studies (209 participants) focused on benign epilepsy of childhood with centrotemporal spikes (BECTS), while one study (146 participants) addressed generalized tonic-clonic seizures (GTCS). STM was compared to placebo and levetiracetam in the BECTS studies and to phenytoin in the GTCS study. One of the BECTS studies was analyzed based solely on the English translation of its abstract, as the full text in English was unavailable. For the primary outcome, the number of participants who discontinued treatment due to seizure recurrence or adverse reactions was significantly higher in the levetiracetam group compared to the STM group (RR 0.32, 95% CI 0.10 to 1.03; 1 study, 43 participants; low-certainty evidence). Regarding seizure freedom, the results were inconclusive (RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.44; 1 study, 43 participants; low-certainty evidence). Reporting of adverse effects was incomplete. In the GTCS study, participants receiving STM were significantly less likely to develop gingival hyperplasia compared to those receiving phenytoin (RR 0.03, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.58; 1 study, 146 participants; low-certainty evidence). No other statistically significant adverse events were observed when STM was compared to phenytoin or placebo. Behavioral disturbances were the most common adverse events when STM was compared to levetiracetam, with similar incidence rates in both groups (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.55; 1 study, 43 participants; low-certainty evidence). No data were reported regarding quality of life. One study was assessed as having a high risk of bias, and another study had an unclear risk of bias due to insufficient information about study design. Only one trial reported effective blinding methods. The risk of bias for the remaining two studies ranged from low to high. The overall certainty of the evidence for the outcomes was rated as low using the GRADE approach. In conclusion, this review provides insufficient evidence to guide clinical practice regarding the use of STM as monotherapy for epilepsy. The small sample sizes, poor methodological quality, and lack of data on critical outcomes limit the ability to draw meaningful conclusions about the efficacy and tolerability of STM. Further trials with larger populations and longer follow-up periods are necessary to determine the clinical utility of STM.
